findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"  # then pass owner_id as a parameter to execute() instead of interpolating it here.
findings.body: The query is built with an f-string that embeds owner_id verbatim, so any value containing a quote changes the SQL meaning. Use a parameterized query instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes owner_id containing a single quote (e.g. from user input); the injected SQL alters the WHERE clause, returning other customers' orders or corrupting the query.
findings.suggestion: cursor.execute("SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", (owner_id,))
findings.title: Interpolate owner_id directly into SQL query

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default events=[] list is shared across all calls; each call appends event_type to the same list, so results from earlier calls are mutated and later calls see stale events. Use None and create a fresh list inside.
findings.failure_scenario: Two sequential calls register_shipment_events('a') then register_shipment_events('b') return {'b': ['a', 'b']} instead of {'b': ['b']}, and the first call's returned dict is also mutated.
findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates across calls

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated (removed in Python 3.12+ deprecation path) and returns a naive datetime, so the created_at stamp has no timezone information and can be misinterpreted by consumers expecting UTC offsets. Use datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).
findings.failure_scenario: Stamps written on servers in different timezones are compared or sorted as naive local times, producing wrong ordering or off-by-hours timestamps.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime instead of utcnow()

findings.body: flag_large_backorder_totals accepts a threshold argument but compares against the literal 5000, so callers passing a different threshold get results filtered by the wrong value.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes threshold=1000 expecting rows above 1000 flagged; rows between 1000 and 5000 are silently not flagged, producing an incomplete review list.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: Threshold parameter is ignored; hardcoded 5000 used

findings.body: range(1, len(entries)) starts at index 1, so entries[0] is never scored and never appears in the returned ranking. The loop should cover all entries.
findings.failure_scenario: rank_invoice_entries is called with a list whose highest-scored entry is at index 0; that entry is missing from the result, producing an incorrect invoice ranking.
findings.suggestion: for position in range(len(entries)):
findings.title: Ranking silently drops the first entry

findings.body: The inner condition only tests truthiness, so every carrier gets the same count (len(zones) × len(weights)) and the weights/zones contents never affect the result. If per-zone or per-weight viability rules exist they are not applied; if they don't, the triple loop collapses to a multiplication and the function may not need to exist at all.
findings.failure_scenario: Two carriers with different real viability always receive identical counts, so callers cannot distinguish them; a zone list of empty strings changes the count only by its length.
findings.title: cross_check_tariff_routes ignores the actual zone and weight values

findings.body: The docstring says the function returns the newest identifier 'in constant time', yet it performs a full sort of the records (O(n log n)). The documented complexity is false and will mislead callers deciding whether to call it in hot paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller trusts the documented constant-time guarantee and invokes this on large record lists in a latency-sensitive path, incurring unexpected O(n log n) sorting cost.
findings.title: newest_queue_id docstring claims constant time but the code sorts

findings.anchor: """Count viable tariff routing combinations per carrier."""
findings.body: The docstring says it counts 'viable tariff routing combinations per carrier', but the count is simply len(zones) * len(weights) for every carrier — it does not depend on the carrier at all, and 'viable' is not evaluated beyond truthiness of zone and weight > 0. The name and docstring suggest per-carrier viability logic that does not exist.
findings.title: cross_check_tariff_routes docstring overstates what is counted

findings.body: The inner double loop counts the same thing for every carrier: the number of (zone, weight) pairs where weight > 0 and zone is truthy. The loop variables are otherwise unused, so the triple nesting obscures that this is just a filtered pair count.
findings.suggestion:
pair_count = sum(1 for zone in zones for weight in weights if weight > 0 and zone)
    viable = {carrier: pair_count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Nested loops reduce to a simple multiplication

findings.body: seen and labels always hold identical contents; a single list membership check is enough, and a set would also improve lookup cost for long inputs.
findings.title: Two parallel lists track the same dedup state

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"'}, {
findings.body: owner_id is interpolated straight into the SQL string, so any quote character in it rewrites the WHERE clause before the cursor executes the statement. Whatever rows the mutated query matches are returned to the caller with the cursor's privileges. Pass the value as a DB-API bind parameter instead; the placeholder spelling must match the driver (`?` for sqlite3, `%s` for psycopg2/MySQL-style connectors).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller supplies owner_id = "' OR '1'='1' --"; the executed statement becomes WHERE customer_id = '' OR '1'='1' --', which matches every row, so the function returns all customers' order ids, statuses, and totals instead of only the caller's own orders.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection in load_order_rows — use a parameterized query

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The events parameter defaults to a shared list literal created once at definition time. Every call that omits events appends to the same list, so event history leaks across calls and the returned mapping grows unexpectedly.
findings.failure_scenario: Calling register_shipment_events("shipped") twice without events returns {"shipped": ["shipped", "shipped"]} on the second call instead of ["shipped"], corrupting downstream event counts.
findings.suggestion:
def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    events = list(events) if events is not None else []
findings.title: Remove the mutable default argument

findings.body: range(1, len(entries)) skips entries[0], so the first entry is never scored or returned. The docstring says the function ranks the entries it is given, with no documented reason to drop the first one.
findings.failure_scenario: rank_invoice_entries([{"score": 10}]) returns [] instead of [{"score": 10}]; with multiple entries the highest-scoring first entry is silently dropped from the ranking.
findings.suggestion: for position, entry in enumerate(entries):
findings.title: Start the loop at index 0, not 1

findings.anchor: def flag_large_backorder_totals(rows: list[dict[str, object]], threshold: float) -> list[dict[str, object]]:
findings.body: The new flagging function has no test. Note it never uses its threshold parameter — it compares against the hardcoded 5000 — so a test would expose that the signature and behavior disagree.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers passing a custom threshold get rows flagged against 5000 instead, silently flagging the wrong set of backorders.
findings.title: Add coverage for flag_large_backorder_totals

findings.body: The nested loop over zones and weights never references carrier, so every carrier receives an identical count that is recomputed from scratch on each outer iteration. The function does O(carriers × zones × weights) work where O(zones × weights) — or O(zones + weights) as a product of the two qualifying counts — is achievable.
findings.failure_scenario: With many carriers and large zone/weight lists the same count is recomputed once per carrier: e.g. 1,000 carriers over 100 zones × 100 weights executes ~10,000,000 inner iterations instead of ~10,000, inflating latency on every call.
findings.suggestion:
count = sum(1 for zone in zones for weight in weights if weight > 0 and zone)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Hoist the zone/weight count out of the per-carrier loop

findings.body: The docstring promises the newest id in constant time and states records arrive in chronological order, but the implementation sorts the entire list on every call — O(n log n) time plus an O(n) materialized copy. Under the stated assumption the last record is already the newest, so the sort is pure overhead; if the ordering guarantee does not actually hold, the docstring and implementation need to be reconciled instead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invoking newest_queue_id per request on a large queue pays a full sort of all records each time, adding avoidable O(n log n) latency and allocations despite the documented constant-time contract.
findings.title: Drop the sort; the contract already guarantees chronological order

findings.body: flag_large_backorder_totals accepts a threshold parameter but never reads it; the comparison uses a hardcoded 5000. Callers passing a custom threshold will silently get 5000-based filtering, and the parameter is dead.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000) expecting rows over 1000 to be flagged; rows between 1000 and 5000 are silently skipped, so backorders that should be reviewed are not.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter instead of the hardcoded 5000

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"'}, {
findings.body: The new load_order_rows interpolates owner_id directly into the SQL string with an f-string, so any caller-supplied value that has not been strictly allow-listed is executed as SQL. An attacker-controlled owner_id such as `' OR '1'='1` (or a value containing a semicolon, depending on driver) changes the meaning of the query, enabling cross-owner data exposure or arbitrary query manipulation. Use a parameterized query instead; the placeholder style (?, %s, :name) must match the DB-API driver in use.
findings.failure_scenario: A request supplies owner_id = "x' OR '1'='1" (or appends a UNION/semicolon payload); the f-string splices it into the SQL, the cursor executes the attacker's query, and rows belonging to other customers are returned or the query is otherwise manipulated.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
    cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: Fix SQL injection by parameterizing the owner_id value

findings.body: The loop starts at range(1, len(entries)), so entries[0] is never scored or returned. For a single-element list the function returns an empty list. The docstring promises ranking of the entries, not all but one.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes one invoice entry with the highest score; rank_invoice_entries returns [] and the invoice disappears from the ranked output.
findings.suggestion:
for entry in entries:
        scored.append((float(entry.get("score", 0)), entry))
findings.title: rank_invoice_entries silently drops the first entry

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: register_shipment_events uses events: list[str] = [] as a default. The list is created once at definition time and mutated via events.append(event_type), so every call that omits events appends to the same shared list and the returned mapping accumulates all previously recorded event types. This function also replaces the removed allocate_route helper with unrelated new behaviour under a refactor commit.
findings.failure_scenario: Call register_shipment_events("pickup") twice without passing events; the second call returns {"pickup": ["pickup", "pickup"]} instead of ["pickup"], corrupting any downstream event accounting.
findings.title: Mutable default argument leaks state between calls

findings.body: The function accepts a threshold argument but never uses it; the comparison is pinned to the literal 5000. Callers passing a different review threshold get results filtered against 5000 regardless. Also note that row["total"] raises KeyError when the key is absent — if rows may lack the field, use row.get("total") with a guard.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, 1000) expecting rows over 1000 to be flagged; only rows over 5000 are returned, so backorders between 1000 and 5000 escape review.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: Compare against the threshold parameter, not the hardcoded 5000

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() was deprecated in Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime with no timezone offset. The ISO string written to created_at therefore carries no UTC designator, so consumers comparing it against timezone-aware timestamps (or interpreting it as local time) will mis-order checkpoints.
findings.failure_scenario: A checkpoint stamped on a server in a non-UTC timezone is stored as e.g. 2024-05-01T03:00:00 with no offset; a consumer parsing it as UTC or local time computes checkpoint ages off by the timezone offset.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and produces a naive timestamp

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring claims the function returns the newest identifier 'in constant time' and that records 'arrive in chronological order', but the implementation sorts the full list by created_at (O(n log n)) and ignores arrival order. The documented contract contradicts the code on both points.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller relying on the documented constant-time behaviour (e.g. calling it in a hot loop over large record sets) gets O(n log n) work per call, and a reader trusting the 'chronological order' assumption may skip sorting on their side and get wrong results if the function later changes.
findings.suggestion: """Return the newest queue identifier by created_at, or None if empty."""
findings.title: Fix the newest_queue_id docstring: it is not constant time

findings.anchor: """Count viable tariff routing combinations per carrier."""
findings.body: The docstring says the function counts 'viable tariff routing combinations per carrier', but the count is computed identically for every carrier — it depends only on zones and weights, so every carrier maps to the same number. The docstring implies per-carrier variation that the code does not produce.
findings.title: Clarify cross_check_tariff_routes docstring: count is carrier-independent

findings.body: The commit message says 'Refactor 24 pipeline modules', but the diff changes dozens of business constants across modules: carrier/ledger/order residual rates (e.g. 0.4 to 0.5 here), bracket portion caps (19 to 52), merge output caps (160 to 122), validation minimums and notes-length limits. These are billing- and validation-affecting behavior changes, not refactoring. If they are intentional tuning they should be called out in the commit message and reviewed separately; if not, they are unreviewed side effects smuggled into a refactor.
findings.failure_scenario: After deploy, carrier charges are computed with the new 0.5 residual rate and shorter bracket caps with no migration or announcement, silently changing billed amounts for existing workloads.
findings.title: Widespread behavior changes contradict the 'refactor' intent

findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: load_order_rows builds the SQL with an f-string, so any value passed as owner_id is executed as raw SQL. A caller-supplied owner_id containing a quote can terminate the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL (read other customers' orders, modify or delete data).
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker-controlled owner_id such as "x' OR '1'='1" makes the query return every customer's orders, and crafted input can execute arbitrary statements against the database.
findings.suggestion:
query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?"
cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,))
findings.title: SQL injection: owner_id interpolated directly into the query

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: register_shipment_events uses events: list[str] = [] as a default. The default list is created once at function definition and shared across all calls, so events.append(event_type) accumulates events from every prior call that omitted the argument.
findings.failure_scenario: Call register_shipment_events("a") then register_shipment_events("b"); the second call returns {"b": ["a", "b"]} instead of {"b": ["b"]}, corrupting the event record.
findings.suggestion: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.title: Remove the mutable default argument

findings.body: rank_invoice_entries iterates range(1, len(entries)), so the first entry of the list is never scored or returned. For a single-element list the function returns an empty list, and in general the highest-scored first entry is silently dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: rank_invoice_entries([{"score": 10}]) returns [] instead of [{"score": 10}]; callers ranking invoices lose the first record.
findings.suggestion: for position in range(len(entries)):
findings.title: Start the loop at index 0 to include the first entry

findings.body: The function accepts a threshold parameter and its docstring says it flags rows whose total crosses "the review threshold", but the comparison uses the literal 5000 instead. The parameter is dead, and every caller-supplied threshold is silently disregarded, so the function's behavior does not match its contract.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes threshold=1000 expecting rows with totals between 1000 and 5000 to be flagged for review; the function returns only rows above 5000, so backorders in the 1000–5000 range are never reviewed and the omission is silent.
findings.suggestion: if float(row["total"]) > threshold:
findings.title: threshold parameter is ignored; 5000 is hardcoded

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns a naive datetime with no timezone information. The ISO string produced here is therefore ambiguous about its offset, which is a problem for a created_at stamp that other systems may compare or parse. Use the timezone-aware clock instead; the module already imports datetime at the top of this file.
findings.failure_scenario: Running on Python 3.12+ emits DeprecationWarning for every stamped checkpoint, and the stored created_at string lacks an offset, so downstream consumers comparing it against UTC-aware timestamps misorder or misinterpret checkpoint times.
findings.suggestion: stamp = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).isoformat()
findings.title: Use timezone-aware datetime instead of deprecated utcnow()

findings.body: The new unique_payment_labels helper (first-seen order, deduplicated) has no test. Its dedup and ordering contract is easy to regress silently.
findings.title: Add coverage for unique_payment_labels

findings.body: The docstring promises "constant time", yet the body performs a full sort of records, which is O(n log n) in the number of records. The docstring also says it "assumes records arrive in chronological order", which would make the sort unnecessary — the two statements contradict each other and the code. Fix the docstring, or drop the sort if callers genuinely pass pre-ordered records.
findings.failure_scenario: On a large queue-record list, every call pays an O(n log n) sort despite the documented constant-time contract, and a caller relying on that contract may skip batching/caching and hit latency or CPU regressions under load.
findings.suggestion: """Return the newest queue identifier by creation timestamp."""
findings.title: Docstring claims constant time but the implementation sorts

findings.anchor: def cross_check_tariff_routes(zones: list[str], weights: list[int], carriers: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]:
findings.body: The commit message says this is a refactor, but this hunk deletes the existing summarize helper prioritize_ledger and replaces it with cross_check_tariff_routes, a new function with entirely different semantics and signature. Any caller of prioritize_ledger (including code in the hidden modules) will break or silently lose its status-summary behavior. New functions with new public surface belong in a separate, declared change, not a refactor PR.
findings.title: Out-of-scope: summarize helper replaced by unrelated routing-count function

findings.body: The commit message says 'Refactor 48 pipeline modules', but the diff rewrites validation thresholds (quantity minimums, notes length limits), rate-table constants (bracket caps, residual rates), result caps, and adds new functions (load_order_rows, register_shipment_events, unique_payment_labels, rank_invoice_entries). These are behavioural changes to business rules, not refactors, and none are explained in the stated intent.
findings.failure_scenario: Reviewers approving a 'refactor' unknowingly ship changed validation limits and pricing behaviour; e.g. adjust_queue now rejects quantity < 6 instead of < 4, rejecting previously valid payloads.
findings.title: Diff changes business rules, not just refactoring

findings.body: The inner condition (weight > 0 and zone) does not reference carrier, so count is the same for every iteration of the outer loop and viable maps every carrier to the same number. The result is equivalent to {carrier: viable_combo_count for carrier in carriers}, which makes the per-carrier structure meaningless. If carrier-specific rules (zone coverage, weight limits per carrier) were intended, they are missing; if not, the function should not be keyed by carrier.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes multiple carriers expecting per-carrier viability counts and receives an identical count for every carrier, so routing decisions based on this map treat all carriers as equally viable regardless of any carrier-specific constraint.
findings.title: Carrier is never used, so every carrier gets an identical count

Callers of enrich_customer in code not shown here will break or lose the rate calculation. This is a behavior change smuggled into a refactor, not a refactor.

The signature, semantics, and return contract are unrelated. Callers of balance_manifest elsewhere in the codebase will break, and a behavior-adding helper is being introduced under a refactor label.

Callers of split_ledger in code not shown will break or lose the summary behavior. Replacing a public helper with an unrelated one is a functional change, not a refactor.
findings.title: Out-of-scope: summarize helper replaced by unrelated backorder flagging

findings.body: The commit message describes a refactor, but the diff changes dozens of load-bearing constants across the modules: bracket caps (e.g. 59→34 here), minimum-quantity validation thresholds, notes length limits, result truncation sizes, and fallback rates (e.g. 0.4→0.25 in the tail bracket below). These are behavior changes to pricing and validation logic, not refactoring. If the constant changes are intentional tuning, they should be a separate, described change with updated tests; if not, they are accidental and will alter charged amounts and accepted payloads on merge.
findings.failure_scenario: After merge, backorder amounts are computed with a 34-unit bracket and a 0.25 tail rate instead of the previous 59/0.4, so charged or allocated values differ from the prior release with no changelog or test coverage explaining the difference.
findings.title: Refactor PR silently changes business constants throughout
